summary: Specifies how to carry Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) encoded speech in RTP packets. It is designed to interoperate with existing AMR transport formats on non-IP networks, and it also defines a file format for storing AMR speech. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary:
AMR and AMR-WB are speech codecs that compress voice into small pieces and can change their compression rate during a call. This RFC says how those pieces are packed into RTP packets, so that the audio arrives in the right order with the right information attached.

It defines two packing styles. The compact one saves bits. The aligned one is easier to implement and can carry extra protection against lost or damaged data. The RFC also defines a file format, with a short text marker at the start, for storing the same speech as an email attachment.

subtitle: How to pack AMR and AMR-WB speech into RTP packets, and how to store it in files.

tldr.problem: AMR and AMR-WB speech is produced in small 20 ms frames of compressed audio, and there was no agreed way to put those frames into RTP packets so that a sender, a receiver and a gateway between a mobile network and the Internet all agree on what they are carrying.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an RTP payload made of a small header, a table of contents listing each frame, and the frame data itself, in either a bandwidth-efficient form or an octet-aligned form. It also defines a matching file format, with a magic number header, for storing the same speech in email and other storage applications.
tldr.outcome: The payload format carries several frames per packet, adapts to packet loss and bit errors, and keeps the mode requests used by mobile networks intact across a gateway. It also registers the audio/AMR and audio/AMR-WB media types and obsoletes RFC 3267.

facts.label: Table of contents entry
facts.value: 6 bits in bandwidth-efficient mode, 8 bits in octet-aligned mode

today: RFC 4867 is a Proposed Standard from April 2007. It obsoletes RFC 3267 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It registers the audio/AMR and audio/AMR-WB media types and updates both registrations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 3267 and extends that specification with offer/answer rules.

It specifies the payload format for packetization of AMR and AMR-WB encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). The payload format supports transmission of multiple channels, multiple frames per payload, the use of fast codec mode adaptation, robustness against packet loss and bit errors, and interoperation with existing AMR and AMR-WB transport formats on non-IP networks.

A related file format is specified for transport of AMR and AMR-WB speech data in storage mode applications such as email. Two separate media type registrations are provided, one for AMR and one for AMR-WB.

Although this payload format supports the transport of both AMR and AMR-WB speech, the RFC stresses that AMR and AMR-WB are two different codecs and are always handled as different payload types in RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines how compressed speech is placed inside RTP packets and inside files. AMR and AMR-WB stay separate: a receiver needs to know which of the two it is being sent.

sections.title: The Codecs and Their Modes
sections.content:
The AMR codec was developed and standardized by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute for GSM cellular systems, and is now chosen by the Third Generation Partnership Project as the mandatory codec for third generation cellular systems. It is a multi-mode codec supporting eight narrow band speech encoding modes with bit rates between 4.75 and 12.2 kbps. The sampling frequency is 8000 Hz and encoding is performed on 20 ms speech frames, so each encoded frame represents 160 samples of the original speech.

AMR-WB was originally developed by 3GPP for GSM and 3G systems. It supports nine wide band speech coding modes with bit rates ranging from 6.6 to 23.85 kbps. The sampling frequency is 16000 Hz and processing is again done on 20 ms frames, so each encoded frame represents 320 speech samples.

The multi-rate capability is designed to preserve high speech quality over a wide range of transmission conditions. To change mode, the decoder signals the encoder the new mode it prefers; that signal is the Codec Mode Request, or CMR. Because speech usually flows in both directions, the CMR is piggy-backed over the speech frames in the reverse direction, so no out-of-band signalling is needed. Every implementation is required to support all the coding modes and to handle mode switching to any mode at any time, though a transport system may limit which modes may be used and how often a change may happen. The decoder may also use out-of-band means to restrict mode changes to a subset, to set a minimum number of frames between two mode changes, and to limit changes to neighbouring modes.

Both codecs also support voice activity detection and generation of comfort noise parameters during silence. Sending those parameters at regular intervals during silence is called discontinuous transmission. The frames that carry only comfort noise parameters are called Silence Indicator frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Both codecs work in the same way: they compress 20 ms of speech at a time, and they can switch to a lower or higher bit rate as the quality of the connection changes. The receiver asks for a particular rate by putting a short field in the speech it sends back.

sections.title: Unequal Error Detection and Protection
sections.content:
The speech bits in each AMR or AMR-WB frame differ in how sensitive they are to bit errors. Cellular systems have exploited this with unequal error protection and detection, which focus protection on the perceptually most sensitive bits. The bits of a frame are divided into class A, B and C, where class A bits are the most sensitive and class C the least. A frame is only declared damaged if errors are found in the class A bits; errors in the class B and C bits are acceptable. A damaged frame is still useful for error concealment at the decoder, since some of the less sensitive bits can still be used, and this can improve speech quality compared with discarding the frame.

The RTP payload format is designed to let an IP network exploit this, although the use of unequal error protection and detection is optional. One approach is to use a partial checksum that covers the IP, transport protocol, RTP and payload headers, and the most important speech bits, with at least all class A bits covered. The other approach uses a partial checksum for the headers only, plus an AMR or AMR-WB frame CRC that covers the class A bits of each speech frame in the payload.

The first approach is bit efficient, flexible and simple, but a bit error in a protected speech bit causes the whole payload to be discarded, and when several frames share one payload a single bit error can throw away all of them. A frame-wise CRC avoids both problems at the cost of some overhead: it lets the receiver detect errors in class A bits and still use the frame for error concealment, and it stops one bad frame from discarding all the others. The choice between the two depends on available bandwidth and the desired tolerance to bit errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Not all bits in a speech frame matter equally. The format lets a network check only the bits that matter most, so a small corruption does not throw away the whole packet. A per-frame checksum is the extra option that protects each frame separately.

sections.title: The RTP Payload Structure
sections.content:
The complete payload consists of a payload header, a payload table of contents, and speech data representing one or more speech frame-blocks. A payload containing more than one speech frame-block is called a compound payload.

The AMR and AMR-WB payload formats have identical structure, so they are specified together; the only differences are in the types of codec frames contained in the payload.

In bandwidth-efficient mode the payload header is simply a 4-bit codec mode request. The value of the CMR field is the frame type index of the speech mode being requested, which may be 0 to 7 for AMR or 0 to 8 for AMR-WB. A CMR value of 15 indicates that no mode request is present, and other values are for future use. The CMR must be set to 15 for packets sent to a multicast group.

The table of contents is a list of entries, one for each speech frame. In bandwidth-efficient mode each entry is 6 bits: an F bit that is set to 1 when another frame follows in this payload, a 4-bit FT field holding the frame type index, and a Q bit giving the frame quality indicator. FT=14, which is only available for AMR-WB, means the frame was lost, and FT=15 means no data is present for that frame in this payload. If a receiver gets an FT value in the range 9 to 14 for AMR, or 10 to 13 for AMR-WB, it should discard the whole packet, to avoid losing data synchronization during depacketization.

The payload is built by packing the header, the table of contents and the speech frames in order, and adding 0 to 7 zero padding bits to reach octet alignment. With N channels and K frame-blocks in a packet there must be N*K entries in the table of contents, the first N entries coming from the first frame-block.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet starts with a short header saying which speech rate is wanted, then a list, one entry per speech frame, saying what kind of frame each one is and whether it is damaged. The compressed frames follow in the order the list gives.

sections.title: Octet-Aligned Mode, Interleaving and Frame CRCs
sections.content:
In the octet-aligned format, all the fields in a payload, including the payload header, the table of contents entries and the speech frames themselves, are individually aligned to octet boundaries to make implementations efficient. In the bandwidth-efficient format only the full payload is octet aligned, so fewer padding bits are added. Between the two operation modes, only the octet-aligned mode has the capability to use robust sorting, interleaving and frame CRC.

In octet-aligned mode the payload header holds the 4-bit CMR, four reserved bits that must be set to zero and ignored on receipt, and an optional 8-bit interleaving header. The ILL field gives the interleaving length as L+1 frame-blocks, and the ILP field gives the interleaving index of the frame-blocks in this payload. If ILP is found greater than ILL the payload should be discarded. Interleaving must be performed on a frame-block basis, not on a frame basis, in a multi-channel session. All payloads in an interleaving group must have the same ILL and the same number of frame-blocks, and the sender must only apply interleaving if the receiver has signalled its use.

The table of contents entry in octet-aligned mode is 8 bits: the same F, FT and Q fields as before, plus two padding bits. The list of frame CRCs is optional and exists only if the use of CRC is signalled out-of-band for the session. When present, each CRC is 8 bits long and corresponds to a speech frame, not a frame-block. The CRC must be calculated only over the class A bits of the frame; class B and C bits must not be included in the CRC calculation and should not be covered by the transport checksum.

Interleaving spreads consecutive losses into a series of single frame-block losses, which usually sounds better than losing several consecutive blocks, at the cost of increased end-to-end delay. Streaming applications are the ones most likely to benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: The octet-aligned version pads every field to a whole number of bytes, which makes an implementation simpler. It also has room for two extras: a checksum per speech frame, and a way of spreading consecutive frames across several packets so that one lost packet does not blank out a stretch of speech.

sections.title: The Storage Format
sections.content:
The storage format is used for storing AMR or AMR-WB speech frames in a file or as an email attachment, and supports multiple channel content. A file has a header followed by the speech frames in order.

A single-channel file header contains only a magic number, and different magic numbers distinguish AMR from AMR-WB. The magic number for single-channel AMR files must be the ASCII string #!AMR , or 0x2321414d520a in hexadecimal, and for single-channel AMR-WB files #!AMR-WB , or 0x2321414d522d57420a. The newline is an important part of the magic number and must be included in the comparison, since otherwise the single-channel magic numbers would become indistinguishable from the multi-channel ones.

A multi-channel file header consists of a magic number followed by a 32-bit channel description field. The multi-channel AMR magic number is #!AMR_MC1.0 and the AMR-WB one is #!AMR-WB_MC1.0 ; the version number in the magic numbers refers to the version of the file format. In the channel description field, the CHAN field is a 4-bit unsigned integer giving the number of audio channels in the file, and the remaining reserved bits must be set to zero when written and ignored by a reader.

After the header, speech frame-blocks consecutive in time are stored, each containing as many octet-aligned speech frames as there are channels, in increasing order starting with channel 1. Each stored frame starts with a one-octet frame header holding the same FT and Q fields as the table of contents entry, followed by the speech bits. The last octet of each frame is padded with zeroes if needed. Frames or frame-blocks lost in transmission must be stored as NO_DATA frames, or as SPEECH_LOST in complete frame-blocks, to keep synchronization with the original media.
sections.plainLanguage: A stored file starts with a short text marker that says which codec it holds and how many channels it has. After that come the speech frames one after another, each with a one-byte label saying what kind of frame it is.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
The RFC defines the parameters that select optional features of the payload formats, as part of the media type registrations for the AMR and AMR-WB speech codecs. Two separate registrations are made, one for AMR and one for AMR-WB, because they are distinct encodings that must be distinguished by their own media type. The registrations follow RFC 4855 and the media registration rules.

The AMR registration uses the media type audio with subtype AMR and no required parameters. The optional parameters are octet-align, which selects octet-aligned operation; mode-set, which restricts the active codec mode set to a comma separated list of modes from 0 to 7; mode-change-period, which sets the frame-block period at which codec mode changes are allowed, to either 1 or 2; mode-change-capability, which says whether the client can transmit with a restricted mode change period; mode-change-neighbor, which recommends that the sender only perform mode changes to the neighbouring modes in the active set; and maxptime, the maximum amount of media that can be encapsulated in a payload packet, expressed in milliseconds.

A mapping of the parameters into the Session Description Protocol is provided for applications that use SDP, together with offer/answer rules for negotiating them. The RFC notes that the AMR-WB registration also adds parameters for the wideband case, and that unspecified parameters must be ignored by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: The two media types, audio/AMR and audio/AMR-WB, carry a few extra settings: whether to use the aligned format, which speech rates are allowed, and how often the rate may change. These are negotiated between the two ends when the session is set up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the general security considerations discussed for RTP and for any profile in use, such as AVP or SAVP. As the format transports encoded speech, the main security issues are confidentiality, authentication and integrity of the speech itself. The payload format has no built-in security mechanisms, so external mechanisms such as SRTP are needed. The RFC recommends SRTP where it is suitable, and notes that IPsec and TLS are other known possibilities.

To achieve confidentiality of the encoded speech, all speech data bits need to be encrypted. There is less need to encrypt the payload header or the table of contents, because they only carry the requested speech mode, the frame type and the frame quality, and that information may be useful to a third party such as a quality monitoring system. Because packetization and unpacketization happen only at the endpoints, encryption should be performed after packet encapsulation and decryption before packet decapsulation. A change of keys should occur at the boundary between interleaving groups, otherwise speech quality degrades for the whole interleaving group.

To authenticate the sender and protect the integrity of the packets in transit, an external mechanism has to be used, and SRTP is recommended again. The use of unequal error detection and protection may be difficult to combine with some integrity protection mechanisms, because any bit errors will cause the integrity check to fail. Data tampering by a man-in-the-middle attacker could cause erroneous depacketization or decoding, and tampering with the CMR field may result in a different speech quality than desired.
sections.plainLanguage: The format itself does not encrypt anything. To keep the conversation private and to stop anyone altering it in transit, the RFC recommends running the stream under SRTP, the encrypted version of RTP.
